newsitem.title: DUBAI: EU ambassadors to return to Iran soon - diplomats.
newsitem.headline: EU ambassadors to return to Iran soon - diplomats.

text.p: European ambassadors will start returning to Tehran as early as this week, barely three weeks after being recalled when a German court cited Iran's rulers ordering political assassinations, European diplomats in Iran said on Monday.

Though European Union foreign ministers on Tuesday are expected to keep their policy of "critical dialogue" with Iran under suspension, the return of ambassadors can be seen as a sign the EU is reluctant to damage lucrative ties with Iran, they said.

The United States again this month urged the 15-member EU to take a hard line against Tehran and join economic sanctions Washington has imposed on Iran for alleged sponsorship of international terrorism. Iran denies the charges.
"We expect our ambassador to return on May 1 or at the end of this week," said a diplomat at one EU embassy in Tehran.
"The ambassador was asked to return for consultations. He is now ready to resume his duties," said another European diplomat.
A third diplomat said that EU capitals would be coordinating the return of their ambassadorial staff and the first heads of missions could go back before the end of this week.
EU governments except Greece recalled their envoys for consultations after a Berlin court on April 10 accused Tehran of ordering the 1992 murder of four Kurdish dissidents.
Tehran has denied any involvement and expelled four German diplomats after Bonn kicked out four Iranian diplomats.

European foreign ministers meeting in Luxembourg are expected to discuss a draft proposal that would accuse Iran of conducting state terrorism, break off high-level meetings with Tehran and exclude top Iranian officials from EU states.
Iran's Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati has said he was not worried about ties with Europe.

"We do not have any expectations from them (EU). They are entitled to make a decision on their own and we will announce our stand toward their decision later on," Velayati said on Sunday in comments carried by the official Iranian news agency.
State-run Tehran radio on Monday said: "It appears that the EU has lost its past enthusiasm in dealing negatively with Iran and is instead seeking to...maintain its ties with Iran."

In the weeks following the Berlin verdict European leaders, particularly in Germany and France, have been at pains to stress the need to maintain links with Iran, the most populous Gulf state and the world's third largest oil exporter.
"The attitude in Iran, even since April 10, has been fairly relaxed...there has been no hostility," said a diplomat.

The EU is Tehran's biggest trading partner and it relies on Iran for 10 percent of its oil imports. Bilateral trade with Germany was just short of $2 billion in 1996 while France's most public investment is Paris-based oil firm Total SA's current development of two Iranian oil and gas fields.
Iran's official media said this month that Iran could turn to Asia for its trade if EU states did not follow a policy independent of the United States and arch foe Israel.

An early return of ambassadors would also help missions monitor Iranian presidential elections on May 23 which will see current incumbent President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani step down after eight years in office, the diplomats said.
